shortDescription: At Rome and in Egypt, the teacher Valentinus and his students told of a highest God, the Father of all, above a lesser maker of this world. They taught that the Savior came to make that Father known.

timeline.headline: Basilides writes, and Valentinus comes to Rome

lines.text: Clement of Alexandria writes that the founders of the heresies arose in the times of the emperor Hadrian and lasted into the age of Antoninus, among them Basilides. Basilides' followers boast that his teacher was Glaucias, the interpreter of Peter.
lines.reference: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata VII.17, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 52955-52960

lines.text: Clement writes that Valentinus' followers claim he was a hearer of Theudas, a pupil of Paul.
lines.reference: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata VII.17, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 52962-52967
lines.note: His followers' claim, as Clement reports it.

lines.text: Clement quotes Basilides, in the twenty-third book of his Exegetics, on why martyrs suffer: those who sinned unawares in other things, he says, are brought to this good end by the kindness of the one who leads them.
lines.reference: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata IV.12, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 38952-38957

lines.when: in the time of Hyginus, bishop of Rome
lines.text: Irenaeus writes that Valentinus came to Rome in the time of Hyginus, flourished under Pius, and stayed until Anicetus.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.4.3, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 39969-39970
lines.note: Irenaeus, a bishop and an opponent, wrote later in the same century.

lines.when: about 140, the third year of Antoninus
lines.text: Eusebius's Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, says that while Hyginus was bishop of Rome, Valentinus the heretic and Cerdo, Marcion's teacher, came to Rome.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, cic/texts/jerome_eusebii-chronici-canones-lat_fotheringham1923.txt lines 42747-42750; the year is a conversion, worked out from the Chronicle's own date, the third year of Antoninus, counting his reign from 138
lines.note: Written more than two centuries later.

lines.when: about 143, the sixth year of Antoninus
lines.text: The Chronicle says Valentinus the heretic becomes known, and remains until Anicetus.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Chronicle, in Jerome's Latin, cic/texts/jerome_eusebii-chronici-canones-lat_fotheringham1923.txt lines 42765-42769; the year is a conversion, counting Antoninus's reign from 138

lines.text: Epiphanius heard that some said Valentinus was born on the coast of Egypt and was taught Greek learning at Alexandria. He calls the report uncertain.
lines.reference: Epiphanius, Panarion 31.2, cic/texts/epiphanius_ancoratus-panarion-haer-1-33-gcs-bd1-grc_holl1915.txt lines 28941-28948

timeline.headline: Valentinus breaks with the church, and his followers are named after him

lines.text: Justin writes that his own people name some who call themselves Christians after the men their teaching came from: Marcians, Valentinians, Basilidians and Saturnilians.
lines.reference: Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 35, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 19244-19256

lines.text: Tertullian writes that Valentinus had hoped to become a bishop, being able in mind and speech. When another man won the place by a claim his suffering for the faith had given him, Valentinus broke with the church.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 43109-43113; Latin, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars3-lat_kroymann-csel47.txt lines 9633-9634, 9652-9653
lines.note: Tertullian's account, an opponent's. He names no city.

lines.text: Tertullian writes that Marcion and Valentinus were at first believers in the church of Rome, and were expelled more than once for their restless curiosity, which spread to the brethren.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Prescription Against Heretics 30, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 21331-21339
lines.note: Tertullian names the bishop of Rome then as Eleutherus.

lines.text: Irenaeus writes that Polycarp, coming to Rome in the time of Anicetus, turned many away from Valentinus and Marcion to the church.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.3.4, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 39869-39873

timeline.headline: Valentinus teaches of paired powers above the world, and of a heart made pure

lines.text: Irenaeus writes that Valentinus taught of a first pair beyond naming, the Unspeakable and Silence. From them came Father and Truth, then Word and Life, Man and Church, and more powers after them.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.11.1, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 31520-31530

lines.text: One of the twelve powers that came from Man and Church, Irenaeus writes, fell from its place and brought forth the rest of the universe. A mother shut out of the fullness, the realm of these powers, bore Christ, and then another son, the Demiurge, or craftsman, ruler of all below him.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.11.1, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 31529-31543

lines.text: In a letter, Valentinus writes that the heart, home to many spirits, is like an inn full of holes and filled with dung. When the only good Father visits it, it is made holy and gleams with light.
lines.reference: Valentinus, in Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II.20, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 34289-34303
lines.note: His own words, kept by Clement.

lines.text: In a homily, Valentinus writes: you are immortal from the beginning, children of eternal life, and you wished death to be given to you, so that death might die in you and through you.
lines.reference: Valentinus, in Clement of Alexandria, Stromata IV.13, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 39090-39095
lines.note: The English print names the author Valentinian.

lines.text: Clement writes that the followers of Valentinus leave faith to the simple, and say knowledge springs up in themselves, who are saved by nature.
lines.reference: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II.3, cic/texts/anf02_hermas-tatian-athenagoras-theophilus-clement-alexandria.xml lines 32105-32109

lines.text: Tertullian writes that Valentinus kept the powers within God himself, as his thoughts, feelings and motions, and that Ptolemy later made them persons outside God.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 43117-43121; Latin, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars3-lat_kroymann-csel47.txt lines 9656-9660

timeline.headline: His students spread the teaching, and Irenaeus writes against them

lines.when: while Eleutherius is bishop of Rome, the twelfth from the apostles
lines.text: Irenaeus writes Against Heresies, especially against the disciples of Ptolemy, whose school he calls a bud from that of Valentinus.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I, preface 2, and III.3.3, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 29871-29873, 39849-39851

lines.text: Irenaeus writes that those from Valentinus speak to church members, whom they call common and churchly, and ask why they are called heretics when they hold the same teaching. To those they win, they then tell in private the mystery of their fullness.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.15.2, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 42121-42141

lines.text: Irenaeus writes that those from Valentinus call a recent writing of theirs the Gospel of Truth, which, he says, agrees in nothing with the apostles' Gospels.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.11.9, cic/texts/anf01_apostolic-fathers-justin-irenaeus.xml lines 41173-41178

lines.text: Ptolemy writes to a woman named Flora that the law of Moses was given neither by the perfect God nor by the devil. Its giver, he says, is the maker of this world, who stands between them, less than the perfect God, and is rightly called just.
lines.reference: Ptolemy, Letter to Flora, in Epiphanius, Panarion 33.3 and 33.7, cic/texts/epiphanius_ancoratus-panarion-haer-1-33-gcs-bd1-grc_holl1915.txt lines 34016-34017, 34658-34672
lines.note: Ptolemy's own words. Epiphanius, an opponent, copied the letter whole. The Greek print is damaged.

lines.text: Ptolemy tells Flora that the Father of all was made known only by the one who came, and that she will learn more if found worthy of the apostolic tradition, which, he says, they too received by succession.
lines.reference: Ptolemy, Letter to Flora, in Epiphanius, Panarion 33.3 and 33.7, cic/texts/epiphanius_ancoratus-panarion-haer-1-33-gcs-bd1-grc_holl1915.txt lines 34162-34163, 34729-34732

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Bardaisan was at first a follower of Valentinus, but later rejected his teaching.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History IV.30.3, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 26652-26655

timeline.headline: The schools divide, and Tertullian, Hippolytus and Origen answer them

lines.text: Tertullian writes that the Valentinians guard their teaching in silence, like the Eleusinian mysteries, the secret rites of Athens, and commit no secret even to their own disciples until they are sure of them. Asked a plain question, he says, they answer that the subject is profound.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 1, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 42928-42930, 42950-42974

lines.text: Tertullian writes that they brand the Christians of the church as simple.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 2, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml line 42981

lines.text: Tertullian writes that Heracleon, Secundus and Marcus the magician each struck out paths of their own, and Theotimus worked on the images of the law. Only Axionicus, at Antioch, keeps Valentinus' rules in full.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 43121-43128; Latin, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars3-lat_kroymann-csel47.txt lines 9660-9666

lines.text: Tertullian writes that his side calls them Valentinians, though they disavow the name, and that they have departed from their founder while keeping their origin.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 43104-43108; Latin, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars3-lat_kroymann-csel47.txt lines 9630-9633

lines.text: After his pupils' new paths, Tertullian writes, Valentinus is now nowhere, yet there are still Valentinians, named through Valentinus.
lines.reference: Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4, Latin, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars3-lat_kroymann-csel47.txt lines 9663-9664
lines.note: Rendered from the Latin, which the English print misreads (line 43124).

lines.text: Hippolytus writes that the school divided into an Italian branch, of Heracleon and Ptolemy, who said the body of Jesus was of soul, and an Eastern branch, of Axionicus and Bardesianes, who said it was spiritual.
lines.reference: Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies VI.35, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 9641-9663

lines.text: Origen answers Heracleon, said to be a friend of Valentinus, on the Gospel of John. Heracleon reads Capernaum, where Jesus went down, as the farthest parts of the world, the regions of matter into which he came down.
lines.reference: Origen, Commentary on John II.8 and X.11, cic/texts/anf09_gospel-of-peter-diatessaron-origen-commentaries.xml lines 23164-23170, 27710-27715

timeline.headline: Bishops and an emperor name the Valentinians among the heretics

lines.text: Cyprian of Carthage names the Valentinians among the heretics, those who, their enemies said, chose error, and says they could share one baptism with his church only if they confessed the same Father, Son and Holy Spirit and the same church.
lines.reference: Cyprian, Letter to Jubaianus 4-5, cic/texts/anf05_hippolytus-cyprian-caius-novatian.xml lines 38515-38524, 38546-38548; heretics, from the Greek for a choice, Tertullian, Prescription Against Heretics 6, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 20274-20279

lines.text: Constantine's edict to the heretics names the Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites, Paulians and Cataphrygians, and takes the houses where they meet.
lines.reference: Constantine, edict to the heretics, in Eusebius, Life of Constantine III.64-65, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 66068-66080, 66124-66128; Greek, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd1-vita-constantini-oratio-ad-sanctos-grc_heikel1902.txt lines 13035-13039

lines.text: Epiphanius writes that Valentinus preached in Egypt, where his seed, like a viper's bones, still remains in several districts. He preached at Rome too, and in Cyprus, Epiphanius says, he left the faith.
lines.reference: Epiphanius, Panarion 31.7, cic/texts/epiphanius_ancoratus-panarion-haer-1-33-gcs-bd1-grc_holl1915.txt lines 29762-29768, 29802-29806
lines.note: Written late in the 4th century. The Greek print is damaged.

uncertain: When Valentinus was at Rome. Irenaeus says he came in the time of Bishop Hyginus, flourished under Pius and stayed until Anicetus. Tertullian says he and Marcion were believers in the church of Rome under Bishop Eleutherus before they were expelled.

Why he broke with the church. Only Tertullian, an opponent, gives a reason: Valentinus had hoped to become a bishop, and another man won the place by the claim his suffering for the faith had given him. Tertullian names no city, and says such men are often roused by ambition to revenge.

Where he came from. Epiphanius, late in the 4th century, heard that some said he was born on the coast of Egypt and schooled in Greek learning at Alexandria, and he calls the report uncertain. He also says Valentinus left the faith in Cyprus, while Irenaeus says he stayed at Rome until Anicetus.
His teacher. Clement says the followers of Valentinus claimed he had heard Theudas, a pupil of Paul, and that the followers of Basilides claimed Glaucias, the interpreter of Peter.

What is his and what is his school's. Irenaeus gives a short account of Valentinus' own teaching and a much longer one of Ptolemy's school. Tertullian says Valentinus kept the powers within God, and Ptolemy made them persons outside God.
The Gospel of Truth. Irenaeus says those from Valentinus called a recent writing of theirs the Gospel of Truth. The old sources held here do not say who wrote it.
Teaching in private. Irenaeus and Tertullian, both opponents, say the Valentinians first won hearers in the churches and told them their deeper teaching only later, in private.
Their own words. The words of Valentinus, Ptolemy and Heracleon held here survive only as their opponents copied them: Clement, Epiphanius and Origen.
